scope: the six functional-family lanes (clean, clojure, elixir, erlang, fsharp, haskell); the shape extends to any lane with an entry in script/m14/verify-grammar-pins.ts
rule: A pinned grammar is its wired bytes (sha256+length), its enumerable surface (id-order, type-set and field-set digests through web-tree-sitter, with the id/named/anonymous vocabularies recorded separately), the local copies those bytes are byte-identical to, the vendored source files (per-file sha256), and the authored provenance/decision record. Verification re-measures all of it and fails on ANY drift — including a vendored source edit, a vanished copy, or a name the vendored source declares that the wired wasm does not have. Regenerating the record is an explicit act (--write), never a silent side effect of verifying.

patches: keyframe_block: add float_value to the step choice — `33.3%` is a float_value, not an integer_value, and float_value already exists in this grammar, so no node type is added (measured 151 -> 151). Repro: @keyframes f { 33.3% { color: yellow } }

plain_value: allow a LEADING `.` — an unquoted relative url() could not lex at all, because the token ended at the first `.` and the `..` became two ERROR nodes; `.` was already legal in the token's BODY, so only the leading repeat lacked it. source.note: grammar.js (PATCHED — see provenance.patches) + src/scanner.c + src/tree_sitter/{parser,alloc,array}.h + package.json + tree-sitter.json + LICENSE + README.md. The grammar source is byte-for-byte from the npm tree-sitter-powershell@0.26.4 tarball EXCEPT grammar.js, which carries one additive hunk; `tree-sitter diff` against the tarball's own grammar.js is the record of what changed, and it is three rules and no edit to an existing one. The generated src/parser.c (4.5 MB) is NOT vendored: `tree-sitter generate` rebuilds it, and the source↔wasm check runs on the generated JSONs, never on parser.c. Unlike the css/cpp vendors this lane's src/ holds only the hand-written scanner, so the .gitignore rule that drops `grammars/tree-sitter-*/src/*` — the rule that silently cost cpp its scanner and css its own (see the two negations above) — needed a THIRD negation for this lane, because tree-sitter-powershell's external scanner is also named src/scanner.c. The same trap, a third time, named by filename rather than by role.

powershell.decision: Pin the patched local rebuild, and record both decisions that got here, because both were measured and one of them was a correction. (1) The BASE was identified by fetching all four published versions and hash-matching: the wired bytes were tree-sitter-powershell@0.25.10 (sha 1d30b5a2…, 983,236 B), not the 0.26.4 sitting in the npm cache. The only thing that said so was the full id enumeration — 415 ids vs 419, id-order digests differing, and a source diff naming `_string_literal_immediate`, the here-string fix. The NAMED vocabularies are identical (152), so a pin comparing named types alone would have passed two revisions as one, and the first grammar hunk would have been written against a grammar the product does not load. (2) The 0.25.10 → 0.26.4 upgrade was measured before it was taken: 0 files fixed, 0 broken over 73 production corpus files, identical 152 named types and 14 fields, 2 fewer ERROR nodes in ansible. (3) The PATCH is G5, and its provenance is stronger than any other lane's because the base was PROVEN before it was patched: the unpatched 0.26.4 source rebuilds to the published prebuild BYTE-FOR-BYTE (same 1,088,467 B, same sha), so the patch is a delta against a known artifact rather than against whatever the source happened to be. A rebuild's sha is not a function of its source across toolchain versions (M49 W19), so the patch's own sha is a local build and the ID-ORDER digest is the part that can be required to match — 419 ids / ff141f18453a becomes 423 ids / 50274a750a87 with G5a/b and 425 ids / 2edf2378eb2c with G5c, and the 152 NAMED types are unchanged at every step, which is the property that keeps an analyzer written against the old shapes from being silently re-pointed. (4) BOTH patches are strictly additive to the rules they extend. G5a/b inserts two hidden precedence levels and edits no existing rule. G5c adds one `choice` arm to `member_access`, one to `element_access` and one to `invokation_expression`, changing no precedence number and no existing arm; the operators are `token.immediate` for the same reason the `.` in `member_access` is, so `?.` is not recognised across whitespace and `$c ? .5 : 1.5` cannot be stolen. The one form whose meaning changes is `$c?[1,2] : $y` written tight, which this grammar now reads as null-conditional indexing — which is what PowerShell itself does, so the ambiguity is resolved the way the language resolves it rather than invented here. F11 on the G5c candidate: G1 damage 137 → 135 files and MISSING 177 → 139 with 0 newly damaged, G2 identity 263 clean files with 0 tree differences, and G3 losing exactly ONE (label,target) pair — whose target F11 prints in full as a seven-line ERROR block — against +126 pairs added. That single pair is the same false-negative class as G5b's 135, and the census confirms it: NullConditional.Tests.ps1 falls 69 → 16 ERROR nodes, NativeCommandPathUpdate.Tests.ps1 goes hasError=true → false, and the three corpus files that do not use `?.` are BIT-IDENTICAL between the two grammars.

alternatives.option: G5c as a new precedence level, or `?.[` for element access
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on measurement, and both halves of it came from the corpus rather than from taste. The corpus target disagrees with the documentation on the element-access form: PowerShell's own test/powershell/Language/Operators/NullConditional.Tests.ps1 uses `?[` (6 × `?[0]`, plus `?[tb]`, `?['a']`, `?[-2]`, `?[0..2]`, `?[0,1]`, `?[]`, `?[1234]`) and never `?.[`, so a `?.[` implementation would have satisfied the docs and none of the corpus. And a precedence LEVEL was rejected for the same reason G5a's named levels were: `?.` binds exactly like `.` and `?[` exactly like `[`, so the correct edit is one `choice` arm inside the rule that already defines the twin, inheriting its associativity — which is also what makes the corpus's `${psObj}?.name?.nonExistent` chain and its `(Get-Item $TestDrive)?.EnumerateFiles()?.Name` compose without a new level at all.

alternatives.option: G5 with the two precedence levels left NAMED (the first attempt)
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on measurement, and it is the most instructive rejection in this lane. It scored a clean win on every count the repro battery reports — 2 of 12 named limits fixed, 0 regressions, all 9 controls held — and the collateral gate passed too, 0 files broken. It was still the wrong patch, and only the SHAPE delta caught it: a named level emits its node in the pass-through case as well, so adding two levels wrapped EVERY expression in the language and produced 9,046 `coalesce_expression` and 9,038 `ternary_expression` nodes across 49 corpus files, re-pointing an analyzer written against the old shapes while every other number said 'pure win'. Hiding both levels makes the rules inline, so an expression using neither operator produces exactly the tree it produced before and F11's G2 identity gate passes by construction rather than by luck.

alternatives.option: the previously wired version, tree-sitter-powershell@0.25.10 (sha 1d30b5a21866354aa2eb94845556f1e19126ff00e3335048719a0e6435b1c154, 983,236 bytes)
alternatives.measured: 0.25.10 vs 0.26.4 unpatched, production corpora: damaged files 16/49 powershell and 15/24 ansible on BOTH; ERROR nodes 93 → 91 in ansible; named vocabulary IDENTICAL (152) so no analyzer is re-pointed; 0 files broken. The base upgrade buys the here-string fix and nothing else, which is why it is recorded as taken rather than as a repair.

alternatives.option: patch the source while the wired bytes stay 0.25.10
alternatives.measured: REJECTED, and this is the reason the pin exists. The npm cache held 0.26.4 and the first draft of this lane's review called it the wired grammar's source; it is not. Rebuilding the cache's source gives 419 ids against the wired wasm's 415 and a different id-order digest, so a hunk written against that grammar.js would have been a patch on a DIFFERENT grammar and every A/B number attributed to it would have been unattributable. Found by measuring the surface gap before writing any hunk, not after.
